claims.text: The coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure.
The as-produced coating contains randomly distributed FCC/BCC interphase boundaries.
The as-produced interphase boundaries have moderate coherence.
A controlled heat treatment or processing route is proposed to refine the FCC/BCC interphase boundaries and increase their coherence.
The density, spacing, and coherence of FCC/BCC interphase boundaries govern creep resistance.
FCC/BCC interphase boundaries pin or impede dislocation motion.
Refined, more coherent interphase boundaries obstruct both dislocation glide and dislocation climb.
Interphase-boundary refinement and increased coherence raise the activation energy for creep processes.
Interphase-boundary pinning delays progressive plastic deformation under sustained stress.
Increasing interphase-boundary density and coherence will reduce the steady-state creep strain rate relative to the as-produced baseline.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate at high temperature and high stress when dislocation motion is the primary creep mechanism.
The interphase-pinning effect may diminish above the phase-stability temperature range.
The interphase-pinning effect may diminish when the applied stress activates alternative deformation mechanisms.
A controlled comparison can use compositionally identical baseline and heat-treated coatings tested at constant load, 600°C, for 100 hours in an inert atmosphere.
Failure of the refined samples to show a statistically significant reduction in steady-state creep rate relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of observable dislocation pinning at the interphase boundaries would falsify the proposed mechanism.
